title: Quantum algorithms: A survey of applications and end-to-end complexities (section on pricing financial options)
authors: Alexander M. Dalzell, Sam McArdle, Mario Berta, Przemyslaw Bienias, et al. (full list not transcribed)
year_and_status: arXiv v1 4 Oct 2023, v2 5 Aug 2025; arXiv comment states published as open-access book by Cambridge University Press, April 2025 (publisher page not opened)
what_it_does: Survey with an end-to-end section on option pricing via amplitude estimation. Verified in the v2 PDF text: classical sample counts can be reduced below the naive sigma^2/eps^2, cutting into the quadratic quantum speedup; quasi-Monte Carlo can reach a nearly quadratic speedup over plain MC but, per the survey, gains an exponential dependence on the number of assets that limits its use; MLMC can also reduce samples (with a quantum MLMC counterpart); and, citing Chakrabarti et al., about 10^7 T-layers per second with a code distance supporting 10^10 operations translates to a logical clock of about 50 MHz to compete with classical MC.
corrections: Already in SCREENING_TABLE.md (lane 'Debate/critiques') but absent from the L1 rows; added because it already publishes the qualitative point that QMC and MLMC cut into the quadratic speedup, which C2 and C6 build on.
difference_from_our_paper: States the QMC erosion qualitatively and asserts a curse-of-dimensionality limit; it does not measure RQMC exponents. Our measured near n^-1 RQMC on 48- and 416-dimensional baskets (calls and digitals after smoothing) is direct evidence that the dimensional caveat does not bind for these payoffs, and our knock-out exponents locate where the erosion does not occur. No compiled oracle, no frontier, no calculator.
note: Cite in the introduction and in C2/C6 wording as the published qualitative statement; our contribution is the measurement.

title: Practical advantage beyond the quadratic speedup limit with fully-quantum walks
what_it_does: Fully-quantum Metropolis walks for low-temperature Gibbs sampling of dense Ising (SK) models, claiming about a sixth-degree query speedup over the best classical walk. Complete fault-tolerant compilation of all primitives; classical per-step times measured on CPU and on an NVIDIA H100 NVL GPU, plus FPGA estimates; under identical hardware assumptions the runtime crossover falls from about 10^3 years for conventional (quadratic) quantum walks to under one day. Data and notebooks released.
corrections: New find (not in any earlier screen).
difference_from_our_paper: Closest 2026 instance of measured CPU/GPU classical step time plus full fault-tolerant compilation plus a runtime crossover inside Monte Carlo, but for MCMC sampling with a super-quadratic speedup, not mean estimation for pricing. Classical timing is per Markov step, not time-to-accuracy of an estimator under an accuracy/confidence contract; no RQMC, no option payoff. Its conventional-walk result (crossover about 10^3 years) agrees with the quadratic-is-not-enough verdict.
note: Cite in related work as the nearest measured-GPU versus compiled-quantum Monte Carlo crossover study. It further narrows any methodological novelty claim.
